blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Two required case studies at the scale the syllabus asks for: a densely populated area, the Ganges delta in Bangladesh, and a sparsely populated one, the Namib Desert coast of Namibia.

blocks.heading: Dense: the Ganges delta
blocks.text: The Ganges delta in Bangladesh is one of the densest rural areas on Earth: the country averages around 1125 people per square kilometre (2022) and the delta districts run higher still, with village after village threaded along the embankments between paddy fields. The delta supports its density because annual floods renew the soil for rice, the rivers give water and transport, and three harvests a year are possible, so the same hectare feeds far more people than dryland farming could. That is the pattern the syllabus asks for made concrete: flat, fertile, well-watered land, so people settle everywhere on it, densely and continuously. The density is rural, which is what makes it remarkable: most of the delta's people are farmers, not city dwellers, and the villages sit a few hundred metres apart along the embankments with paddy between them, so the countryside itself carries the density. The same closeness brings the pressures topic 1.1 describes, tiny farms per family and services run past capacity, and it makes land the scarce thing: houses are built on the field edges because farmland is too valuable to build on, and the region's roads thread between fields too narrow to lose.

blocks.heading: Sparse: the Namib coast
blocks.text: The Namib Desert coast of Namibia is sparsely populated: the Erongo and Kunene regions along it hold only a few people per square kilometre, against Windhoek's thousands, because the coast receives under 50 millimetres of rain a year. The sparseness rests on physical limits: with almost no rain, neither crops nor herds can live off the land, and the cold ocean and strong winds make settled farming harder still. The people who do live there cluster at the few places with water or other work, Walvis Bay's port and the uranium mining town of Arandis, so the distribution is one of tiny nodes in a very large emptiness. The nodes survive on engineered water, Walvis Bay's desalination and piped groundwater and Arandis's inland pipeline, and when the engineered water goes, the node goes with it, as the abandoned mine settlements inland of the coast show. The mine at Brandberg West, for instance, closed and its people left, because a settlement cannot outlive its water. This order of events is worth holding on to in an answer: state the rainfall and the soils first, the water engineering second, and the thin services last, and the argument carries itself. The same test works in reverse on a mark-hunting answer, because a cause offered after the consequence has the story running backwards, and an answer that opens with the missing clinics has not yet explained anything.For a learner in Namibia this is a familiar scale of contrast: the whole Namib coast holds fewer people than one Windhoek suburb, though the region is hundreds of kilometres long, and the emptiness between the nodes is grazing for hardy livestock and little else.

blocks.heading: Why the Namib has few services
blocks.text: A sparse population keeps few services, and the order matters: the emptiness comes first, and the thin services follow it. The few people of the Namib coast cannot support schools, clinics and shops within reach of every household, which is a consequence of the low density rather than a cause of it, the same distinction the first half of this topic draws.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The two case studies answer any 7-mark question that names a dense or a sparse area, and they pair: the delta's floods are the river processes of topic 2.2 at work, and the Namib's aridity is the climate of topic 2.5. Namibia's own population clusters on the central plateau and the north, a distribution this topic's factors explain.
